strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: multi-subject, identity-preserving video generation from text and reference images, with clear potential usefulness for controllable video synthesis and editing.

The proposed system combines several plausible components: hierarchical intra-subject/inter-subject/cross-modal attention, VLM-based semantic conditioning, curated multi-source training data, and RL-style post-training for identity and quality rewards.

The paper includes comparisons against relevant open-source and proprietary baselines and reports gains in total score and identity-related metrics. The ablations provide some evidence that hierarchical attention, VLM conditioning, and curated data each contribute to performance.
The dataset construction pipeline and appendix statistics suggest a substantial engineering effort, and the qualitative examples indicate that the model can produce compelling multi-subject videos.
weaknesses: The technical description is too underspecified for a major systems paper. The hierarchical attention is described mostly conceptually, without enough architectural detail, tensor flow, projection/adaptation details, complexity analysis, or clear integration points in Wan/MMDiT to make the method reproducible.

The RL component is a major claimed contribution but is not adequately supported. The reward definitions are vague, the weights and implementation details are omitted, Appendix B.2 is effectively empty, and the ablation table does not isolate the online RL stage despite Figure 5 claiming its importance.

The empirical claims are overstated. Table 1 does not show superiority across all metrics: the method is not best on aesthetics, GmeScore, NaturalScore, and only modestly improves total score over strong baselines. The text repeatedly claims state-of-the-art across all metrics, which is not supported by the reported numbers.

Evaluation breadth and reliability are limited. The benchmark has only 180 subject-text pairs, relies almost entirely on automated metrics including MLLM-based scores, and lacks human preference studies, failure analysis, statistical uncertainty, or evaluation by number/type of subjects and interaction complexity.

There is a serious data/evaluation ambiguity: the model is trained using OpenS2V-Nexus-derived data and evaluated following the OpenS2V-Nexus protocol, but the paper does not clearly establish train/test separation or rule out overlap, which weakens confidence in the reported gains.

Reproducibility is weak. Code/data are only promised for future release, proprietary/generated data sources are used, exact prompts and filtering thresholds are sparse, reward details are missing, and key training hyperparameters beyond iterations/resolution/hardware are absent.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to recent multi-subject video generation work: the paper combines known ingredients such as Wan, VLM conditioning, hierarchical/local-global attention, curated synthetic data, and Flow-GRPO-style training, but does not provide enough analysis to show which aspects are fundamentally new or generally applicable.

Some dataset statistics and presentation details are inconsistent or unclear, such as category counts that do not sum cleanly and broad claims about video editing applications without quantitative evaluation. These are not merely cosmetic because they affect confidence in the experimental evidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: controllable multi-subject video generation with identity preservation, where current text/image-conditioned video models are still weak.

The proposed system combines plausible components: hierarchical intra-subject/inter-subject/cross-modal attention, VLM-based conditioning, data curation, and online RL fine-tuning. The overall direction is technically reasonable.

The manuscript includes comparisons against several relevant open-source and proprietary systems, plus ablations for hierarchical attention, VLM conditioning, and curated data. The reported gains in FaceSim and total score suggest the approach may improve identity preservation.
weaknesses: The empirical support is not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. Evaluation uses only 180 subject-text pairs and is dominated by automatic/MLLM-derived metrics, with no human preference study, statistical significance, failure analysis, or clear assessment of temporal identity drift across longer videos.

The claim of state-of-the-art performance is overstated. In Table 1, the method is not best on several individual metrics: VACE has higher GmeScore, Kling has higher Motion and NaturalScore, and Kling also slightly exceeds the reported NexusScore. The total-score gain over Kling is modest and depends on an unspecified normalized weighted sum.

Key technical details are under-specified. The RL section defines rewards only symbolically as Rqual and Rid, without operational definitions, weights, reward models, rollout settings, stability details, or evidence that reward hacking is avoided. The claimed online RL contribution is also not quantitatively ablated in Table 2.

Novelty is incremental relative to recent multi-subject/video customization work. Hierarchical attention, VLM guidance, curated synthetic data, and RL post-training are sensible combinations, but the paper does not clearly isolate a fundamentally new mechanism beyond recombining known ingredients on top of Wan/DiT-style backbones.

Reproducibility is weak. The model depends on large pretrained components, 16 H20 GPUs, a curated dataset partly built with external/proprietary image editing models, and unreleased code/data. The data curation pipeline lacks enough detail to reproduce filtering, subject decomposition, prompt generation, and quality control.

There is a possible train/test contamination concern: the training data includes OpenS2V-Nexus-derived material, while evaluation follows the OpenS2V-Nexus benchmark protocol. The manuscript does not clearly document disjoint splits or safeguards against overlap.
The zero-shot controllable video editing application is shown only qualitatively, without baselines or metrics, so it reads as an unsupported extension rather than a demonstrated capability.

Presentation quality is below the expected bar in places: grammar errors, formatting issues, vague claims, and small/low-detail qualitative figures make the paper harder to assess and reduce confidence in the care of the experimental reporting.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: multi-subject identity-preserving video generation from text plus multiple reference images. This is a practically useful setting that goes beyond single-subject subject-to-video generation and is well motivated by downstream editing, storytelling, and product-placement use cases.

The proposed system is technically coherent. The hierarchical attention design explicitly separates intra-subject, inter-subject, and cross-modal aggregation, which is a plausible architectural response to the identity-conflict and semantic-composition issues in multi-subject generation. The use of a VLM encoder for richer semantic conditioning is also well aligned with the task.

The empirical results are generally strong. On the reported open-domain benchmark, ID-COMPOSER achieves the best total score among the compared open-source and proprietary systems, with especially favorable FaceSim and NexusScore results. The ablations show consistent drops when removing hierarchical attention, the VLM encoder, or curated data, supporting the main design choices.

The paper includes a reasonably broad comparison set, including Phantom, VACE, SkyReels-A2, Vidu, Pika, and Kling, and the qualitative examples suggest visible improvements in identity preservation and compositional consistency.

The dataset construction effort is a meaningful contribution. The authors describe a multi-source curation pipeline combining OpenS2V-Nexus, synthetic subject decomposition, and high-quality video data, which could be useful to the community if released as promised.
weaknesses: Several central experimental claims are overstated. The text says the method outperforms existing methods across all evaluation metrics, but Table 1 shows ID-COMPOSER is not best on every individual metric: for example, Kling has a higher NaturalScore, VACE has a higher GmeScore in some settings, and some baselines have higher aesthetics. The stronger supported claim is best total score and strong identity-related metrics, not uniform dominance.

The evaluation relies heavily on automated and partly MLLM-derived metrics whose validity for this task is not sufficiently established. NaturalScore and GmeScore depend on large multimodal models, and the paper does not provide enough validation, calibration, or correlation with human preference. For a video generation paper, the absence of a human study is a notable gap.

The benchmark size is relatively small: 180 subject-text pairs. This is useful but not fully convincing for broad claims about open-domain multi-subject generation, especially given the diversity of subjects, interactions, occlusions, and temporal dynamics the task entails.

The online RL component is under-evaluated. The method section presents a composite reward, but key details such as reward weights, exact reward models, optimization schedule, and stability controls are thin. The quantitative ablation table does not isolate online RL, and the evidence for RL is mainly qualitative, making it hard to assess its actual contribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives some architecture and training details, but a 14B DiT plus 7B VLM system trained on 16 H20 GPUs with curated/proprietary-data components is difficult to reproduce. Code, pretrained models, and training data are only promised. Dataset licensing, filtering criteria, and generated-data provenance need clearer treatment.

The novelty is meaningful but somewhat system-compositional. Hierarchical attention, VLM conditioning, curated data, and RL post-training are sensible ingredients, but many are adapted from recent related trends. The paper would be stronger with more precise analysis showing why this particular hierarchy is essential compared with other structured attention or conditioning variants.

The qualitative figures are helpful but compressed and hard to inspect in the PDF. Since the task is video generation, static frame grids only partially demonstrate temporal consistency; the paper depends on supplementary videos for important evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: multi-subject subject-to-video generation with identity preservation, prompt alignment, and temporal coherence. This is a real limitation of current personalized video generators.

The proposed system combines several sensible components: hierarchical intra/inter-subject attention, VLM-grounded conditioning, a curated multi-source training set, and GRPO-style online RL with identity and quality rewards.

The empirical section includes comparisons to several open-source and proprietary systems, component ablations, RL ablations, and a small human preference study. The reported FaceSim and total-score gains over strong baselines suggest the approach has practical merit.
The appendix gives more architectural and reward details than the main paper, including attention-stage ablations and GRPO hyperparameters, which helps clarify the implementation.
weaknesses: The core evidence is weakened by metric circularity. The online RL reward optimizes FaceSim/NexusScore/NaturalScore-style quantities, and evaluation heavily relies on closely related automated metrics, including benchmark-specific or VLM-based scores. This makes it difficult to know how much the method improves real perceptual quality versus optimizing the evaluators.

The claims are overstated relative to Table 1. The paper says ID-CRAFTER achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics, but some metrics are higher for other methods, e.g. Kling has higher Motion than Ours-14B and VACE has higher GmeScore. The overall total-score gain of online RL over the 1.3B base model is also small, 54.33 to 55.16.

Important baselines are missing or underused. The paper cites closely related recent multi-subject video methods such as CINEMA, Concat-ID, PolyVivid, and VideoMage, but the main quantitative table compares mostly against VACE, Phantom, SkyReels, and proprietary systems. This makes the claimed SOTA position uncertain.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The training depends on a large curated dataset with internal high-quality videos, generated subjects from proprietary image models, and MLLM-based filtering/scoring. Although the paper promises release, the manuscript does not provide enough detail to reproduce the data pipeline, total training recipe, or evaluation scoring faithfully.

The novelty is incremental at the method level. Hierarchical attention, VLM conditioning, curated synthetic data, and GRPO/RL fine-tuning are all plausible but largely known ingredients; the contribution is mainly their integration for this task. The paper does not isolate whether the gains come from architecture, data scale/quality, stronger base model, or reward optimization sufficiently convincingly.

The evaluation set is small for the breadth of claims: 180 subject-text pairs and 30 participants/200 questionnaires for human evaluation. The human study lacks details on randomization, participant instructions, statistical significance, video sampling, and whether raters were blinded.

Several presentation and technical clarity issues reduce confidence: unresolved reference text such as “Tab. ??”, grammatical errors, undefined symbols/notations, unclear meaning of the star marker in tables, and limited detail on inference settings for baselines and proprietary systems.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: controllable multi-subject video generation with identity preservation, prompt alignment, and temporal consistency. This is a genuinely useful capability for subject-driven synthesis and editing.

The system combines several plausible components: hierarchical identity attention, VLM-based conditioning, curated multi-source data, and GRPO-style online reward optimization. The overall pipeline is coherent at a high level.

The manuscript includes comparisons against open-source and proprietary baselines, ablations for the attention module, VLM encoder, data curation, and RL reward terms, plus a small human preference study in the supplement.
The reported quantitative results suggest some improvement in total score and identity preservation, especially FaceSim, over several open-source baselines such as Phantom and VACE.
weaknesses: The empirical claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper says ID-CRAFTER achieves state-of-the-art performance across all metrics, but Table 1 shows it is not best on several metrics: Kling has higher Motion, NexusScore, and NaturalScore than the 14B model, VACE-14B has higher GmeScore, and the online RL variant reduces Motion, GmeScore, and NaturalScore compared with the base model.

The online RL contribution is weakly supported. Table 3 shows only a small total-score gain from 54.33 to 55.16 over the SFT baseline, while some metrics degrade. The main improvement is FaceSim, which is also directly part of the reward, making it hard to conclude that RL broadly improves video generation quality rather than optimizing the chosen metrics.

There is substantial metric/reward circularity. The method optimizes FaceSim, NexusScore-like subject consistency, aesthetic score, and a VLM-based naturalness reward, then evaluates heavily with similar automated metrics. The human study is too underspecified and small to resolve this concern: 200 questionnaires from 30 participants, without clear sampling, randomization, statistical testing, or failure-case reporting.

Reproducibility is poor. The method relies on a large curated dataset with an internal high-quality collection, proprietary or nonstandard data generation tools such as Gemini/Nano Banana, VLM-based filtering, and benchmark metrics whose implementation details are incomplete. It is unclear whether an independent group could reproduce either the training data or the reported evaluation.

The novelty is incremental. Hierarchical self/cross-attention, VLM conditioning, synthetic data curation, and GRPO-style post-training are all established directions. The paper does not convincingly isolate a new technical idea beyond combining known ingredients in a large video-generation pipeline.

The evaluation set is limited and underdescribed: only 180 subject-text pairs are used for the main benchmark, and the paper does not clearly characterize the number of subjects per prompt, subject categories, difficulty distribution, or whether hyperparameters/model choices were tuned on related benchmark data.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. Baselines differ in model size, accessibility, training data, and supported conditioning interfaces. The paper includes proprietary systems but gives limited detail on how inputs/prompts were adapted, whether outputs were cherry-picked, or whether the comparisons are fair for multi-reference subject conditioning.

The ablations do not cleanly establish the contribution of each component. Removing curated data, VLM conditioning, or hierarchical attention changes broad parts of the training and conditioning pipeline, so the observed drops do not uniquely validate the proposed mechanisms. The supplement’s stage-wise attention ablation is helpful but still limited to automated scores.

Several presentation and technical inconsistencies reduce confidence: duplicated or inconsistent references, placeholder-style references to very recent/unpublished systems, a broken table reference ('Tab. ??'), grammatical issues in key method descriptions, and qualitative figures that are hard to assess from the paper alone.

The claimed zero-shot controllable video editing application is only qualitatively illustrated and not evaluated quantitatively, despite being presented as a meaningful capability of the architecture.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: multi-subject subject-to-video generation, where identity preservation, prompt adherence, and temporal coherence often conflict. The application area is clearly relevant to CVPR.

The proposed ID-Crafter system is technically plausible and well motivated. The hierarchical identity-preserving attention mechanism separates intra-subject refinement, inter-subject interaction, and cross-modal conditioning, which is a reasonable architectural response to identity leakage in multi-subject settings.

The paper combines several useful ingredients: VLM-grounded semantic conditioning, a curated multi-source training set, and online GRPO-style post-training with identity and quality rewards. While the individual ideas are not entirely new, their integration for compositional multi-subject video generation is valuable.

The empirical results are encouraging. On the OpenS2V-style benchmark, the method improves over strong open-source baselines in total score, FaceSim, NexusScore, and motion-related metrics; the 14B model reaches the best total score in Table 1, and the 1.3B model with online RL substantially improves identity preservation over its SFT baseline.

The ablation studies support the main design choices: removing hierarchical attention, the VLM encoder, curated data, or fidelity/quality reward terms degrades relevant metrics. The supplementary material gives useful architectural and training details, including model component sizes, GRPO hyperparameters, reward definitions, and dataset composition.
The paper includes qualitative comparisons, editing examples, and a human preference study, which are important for a generative video paper where automatic metrics are imperfect.
weaknesses: The strongest concern is evaluation circularity. The online RL reward directly optimizes FaceSim, NexusScore, Aesthetic Score, and NaturalScore-like quantities, while the main evaluation relies heavily on the same or closely related metrics. This makes it difficult to separate genuine perceptual improvement from metric optimization. The human study helps, but its protocol is not detailed enough to fully resolve this concern.

The novelty is moderate rather than high. Hierarchical/cross-attention identity injection, VLM semantic conditioning, curated synthetic data, and RL/reward fine-tuning for diffusion or flow models all have close precedents. The contribution is best characterized as a strong systems integration with task-specific adaptation, not a fundamentally new generative modeling method.

The empirical gains are not uniformly strong. The online RL stage improves the total score only modestly over the SFT baseline in Table 1 and Table 3, and it appears to reduce some metrics such as motion, GmeScore, and NaturalScore in Table 1. Some textual claims of improvement across all metrics are therefore overstated.

Comparisons are somewhat hard to interpret because the method uses a large curated dataset, internal high-quality videos, proprietary or semi-proprietary image generation components, Qwen2.5-VL, Wan-Video initialization, and reward models. It is unclear how much of the gain comes from the proposed architecture versus data scale/quality and foundation-model choices.

Reproducibility is limited. The dataset includes an internal high-quality collection and generated data from systems such as Gemini/Nano Banana; prompts, filtering rules, licensing details, and exact release plans are not sufficiently specified. The paper says the model and dataset will be released, but the current manuscript does not make replication straightforward.

The human preference study is under-described: 200 questionnaires from 30 participants is useful, but the sampling procedure, randomization, interface, statistical significance, rater quality control, and whether videos were anonymized are not reported in enough detail.

Some benchmark claims are too broad. Table 1 shows that proprietary systems remain stronger on some individual metrics, and open-source baselines sometimes outperform the proposed model on specific metrics such as GmeScore. The statement that ID-Crafter achieves state-of-the-art performance across all metrics should be qualified.

There are presentation and polish issues, including grammatical errors, repeated phrasing in the RL motivation, a dangling reference to “Tab. ??”, and occasional unsupported strong language. These are not decisive, but they reduce confidence in the precision of the manuscript.
